CausalChain: Green tea catechins (EGCG) intake -> Dose-dependent modulation of intracellular redox status -> Increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species in cancer stem cells -> Activation of mitochondrial apoptotic pathways (e.g., cytochrome c release, caspase activation) -> Selective induction of apoptosis in cancer stem cells -> Reduction in metastatic potential
Hypothesis: Controlled, moderate dosing of green tea catechins can selectively target cancer stem cells by inducing mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and activating intrinsic apoptotic pathways, thereby reducing the metastatic potential of aggressive tumors.
Abstract: Recent investigations into the multifaceted bioactivities of green tea catechins suggest not only their established antioxidant and anticancer capabilities but also a nuanced dose-dependent interplay between pro-oxidant and anti-oxidant mechanisms. In this context, we propose a novel hypothesis that controlled, moderate dosing of green tea catechins, particularly EGCG, can selectively disrupt redox homeostasis in cancer stem cells. This disruption may impair mitochondrial function, enhance intrinsic apoptotic signaling, and consequently diminish the metastatic potential of aggressive tumors. Our hypothesis provides a framework for future studies aimed at enhancing the specificity and effectiveness of catechin-based adjunct therapies in cancer treatment, particularly by targeting the subpopulation of cells responsible for tumor relapse and metastasis.
